8.34

I. Review: Negation

There are two kinds of negation in German:

  • negation using kein-

  • negation using nicht

Both kinds have been discussed from Chapter 3 on; but now that you’ve been introduced to the concept of non-specific vs. specific nouns (Chapter 5), we can discuss all the applications of kein- and nicht using this framework.


I.1

First, a reminder of what is meant by non-specific vs. specific nouns:

Non-specific nouns refer to general entities (Essen, Geld, Zeit), including plural nouns with no article (Geschäfte, Kinder) and non-specific examples (eine Stadt, ein Kurs).

Specific nouns, by contrast, have a focused reference, indicated by the use of definite articles (das Essen, das Geld, die Zeit), possessive adjectives (seine Geschäfte, unsere Kinder) or a specifying word (dieses Essen). Pronouns are also considered specific, since they refer by definition to something that has already been mentioned.

Compare:

non-specific

specific

Geld

dieses Geld / mein Geld / das Geld von …

Kinder

die Kinder von … / ihre Kinder / diese Kinder

eine Stadt

die Stadt / diese Stadt / unsere Stadt
I.1
label: I.1

content:
I.2

Negating with kein-

To negate a non-specific noun, use kein-. This applies to any non-specific noun used as a predicate noun (nominative), a direct object (accusative) or an indirect object (dative). The endings you use with kein- will depend on the case, gender, and number of the noun following it.


Original:

Negated:

Nom.

Lisa ist eine Freundin von mir.

Aber sie ist keine Freundin von Daniel.

Acc.

Im Süden von Deutschland gibt es Berge.

Im Norden gibt es keine Berge.

Acc.

Er braucht ein Auto.

Aber er kauft kein Auto.

Dat.

Die Orange-Key-Gästeführer° zeigen Besuchern den Campus.

Aber sie zeigen keinen Besuchern die Zimmer im Forbes-Annex.

content:
I.3

Negating with nicht

To negate everything else — specific nouns, pronouns, verbs, adverbs (including gern), adjectives, and prepositional phrases — use nicht.

The position of nicht depends on which of these elements is being negated, and in most situations this is determined as follows:


specific nouns

pronouns

verbs (V1)

 

nicht

adverbs

adjectives

prepositional phrases

In these examples, the elements to be negated are underlined in order to highlight their relation to nicht in the negated version:

Original:

Negated:

Sie kennt meine Freunde.

Sie kennt meine Freunde nicht.

Er hilft mir.

Er hilft mir nicht.

Du bleibst.

Du bleibst nicht.

Er fährt schnell.

Er fährt nicht schnell.

Ihr Zimmer ist sehr groß.

Ihr Zimmer ist nicht sehr groß.

Hast du auf mich gewartet?

Hast du nicht auf mich gewartet?

But: If you really want to emphasize the negation of a specific noun or pronoun — and particularly if you want to follow up with corrective information — then you place nicht before the element to be negated, regardless of what it is, and you emphasize the negated element with intonation as well. The subsequent correction is then introduced with sondern or aber, and can also be emphasized with intonation. Structurally, the phrase looks like this:

nicht X, sondern Y (or)

nicht X, aber …

Here are a few examples – with the italicized elements showing intonational emphasis:

Original:

Negated:

Sie kennt meine Freunde.

Sie kennt nicht meine Freunde, sondern meine Eltern.

Er hilft mir.

Er hilft nicht mir, sondern meinem Bruder.

Sie hat mir eine E-Mail geschickt.

Sie hat mir nicht eine E-Mail geschickt, sondern eine SMS.

Ü8.23
label: Ü8.23

content:
I.4

That’s all well and good, you’re thinking to yourself, as long as the number of elements is kept to a minimum and the sentence is in the present tense. But what happens to the rules governing kein- and nicht when you complicate things with “sentence brackets,” i.e., when you introduce modal verbs, auxiliaries, and past participles?

Nothing, actually.

In sentences with a V1 – V2 structure, nicht and kein- function as they do when there’s only one verb. Nicht precedes or follows the negated element in the middle field, as needed, and kein- still precedes non-specific nouns.

Notice how this works in an example with a specific noun and nicht:

Original:

Er versteht die Frage.

Negated:

Er versteht die Frage nicht.

Negated with modal verb:

Er kann die Frage nicht verstehen

Negated in the perfect tense:

Er hat die Frage nicht verstanden.

Various other elements shift their position, but die Frage nicht remains unchanged.

content:
J. Review: Perfect tense


J.1 Form and meaning


eben°

The Perfect tense consists of an auxiliary (either haben or sein, depending on the verb) and a past participle. In an independent clause, the auxiliary functions as V1, and the past participle functions as V2, appearing at the end of the clause.

Hast du eben was gesagt?

Did you just say something?

Ich habe deine Frage nicht verstanden.

I didn’t understand your question.

Sie hat uns alles erklärt.

She explained everything to us.

Er hat uns zum Fest eingeladen.

He invited us to the celebration.

Der Hund ist draußen geblieben.

The dog stayed outside.

The Perfect tense refers to activities in the past that are “perfected,” i.e., finished and no longer taking place — regardless of when they began or how long they lasted. (Remember: If an activity is ongoing in the speaker’s “present,” German signals this by using the present tense, with a prepositional phrase beginning with seit to indicate either the starting point or the duration of the activity.) The Perfect tense translates into English either with an auxiliary form, or with a one-word past-tense form:

ist … gegangen

has gone / went

hat … gedacht

has thought / thought

hat … diskutiert

has discussed / discussed
